units.passage: Education should not be about adopting every new tool as quickly as possible. The focus should remain on pedagogy and ensuring that technology supports learning goals.
units.why: "The focus should remain on pedagogy and ensuring that technology supports learning goals" states a principle that AI choices serve learning goals (P83); the source says "should", so should, addressed to all.

units.passage: SDS faculty are encouraged to teach students how to thoughtfully and ethically incorporate AI tools to maximize student learning while ensuring that faculty can assess competency against course learning outcomes.
units.why: The same sentence requires that faculty "can assess competency against course learning outcomes"; ties AI use to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Teachers are encouraged, in cooperation with their departmental leaders, curriculum committees, and program directors to make course-level decisions that are appropriate for their specific content and student learning objectives.
units.why: Encourages teachers to make course-level decisions 'appropriate for their specific content and student learning objectives', which ties AI decisions to learning objectives (P83); it also names the consultative route with departments. Chosen over P04 because the focus is alignment with objectives.

units.passage: Revisiting the learning outcomes in your course may help you determine if and how generative AI is appropriate for students in your class.
units.policy: Instructors revisit course learning outcomes to determine if and how generative AI is appropriate for students.
units.why: "Revisiting the learning outcomes in your course may help you determine if and how generative AI is appropriate" ties the AI decision to learning outcomes (P83), and leaves the decision to the instructor.

units.passage: Courses, disciplines, and learning goals differ, and these differences have implications for whether, when, or how students should be using AI in your course
units.why: "Courses, disciplines, and learning goals differ, and these differences have implications for whether, when, or how students should be using AI" ties the AI decision to learning goals, which is P83 (not P04, because the point is the basis of the decision).

units.passage: before we design a policy about AI for our course, we need to start by exploring and articulating for ourselves whether or not artificial intelligence is a meaningful tool for our students to use as they develop the skills we want them to learn
units.why: "we need to start by exploring and articulating for ourselves whether or not artificial intelligence is a meaningful tool for our students" makes the AI decision follow from the skills taught, so P83; addressed to instructors before the course.

units.passage: Below are three steps that can help you do this work. Step 1: Identify the key skills you want students to learn in your course. The first step is to make some notes for yourself about the work that you ask students to do in your course.
units.why: Step 1 tells instructors to "Identify the key skills you want students to learn in your course" as the first step of policy design; it feeds the learning-objectives basis for AI decisions (P83).
units.fit_note: A procedural step that precedes the AI decision rather than a rule about AI itself.

units.passage: The question is not whether students could use AI to do this work, but instead if using AI will help them develop the skill you’re targeting. In some cases, you may find it easy to answer “yes” or “no”, and, in other cases, you may find that you initially have to answer “maybe” until you’ve taken more time to think! There are no right or wrong answers here: the most important thing is to make sure that your students’ learning is your primary consideration
units.why: "The question is not whether students could use AI to do this work, but instead if using AI will help them develop the skill" sets the test for allowing AI: whether it helps develop a skill, so P83.

units.passage: After you’ve considered whether using AI will help students develop the skills you’re targeting, take some time to articulate for yourself why you think the use of artificial intelligence might help or hinder your students’ learning.
units.why: Step 3 asks instructors to "articulate for yourself why you think the use of artificial intelligence might help or hinder your students' learning"; it is reasoning behind the AI decision tied to learning, P83.
units.fit_note: Asks for the instructor's private articulation of reasons, not the decision itself. | P83 is about aligning AI with objectives; this unit adds the step of writing down the reasoning for oneself.

units.passage: As you consider how you can help your students become critical of ChatGPT and other AI interfaces as writing generators, be sure your assignments are still aligned with the learning goals that you have for your students. A word of caution here: while some instructors rush to embrace ChatGPT as a teaching tool, it is unproductive to structure activities that are unrelated to the disciplinary thinking you want students to practice.
units.why: "be sure your assignments are still aligned with the learning goals" ties any AI classroom use to learning objectives, P83.

units.passage: The AI uses you allow or prohibit should reflect the kinds of thinking students need to do for themselves to achieve learning goals.
units.why: The guide says to 'center your policy on learning': allowed or prohibited uses 'should reflect the kinds of thinking students need to do for themselves', tying AI decisions to learning goals (P83).

units.passage: 2 Learning Goals for Students: Generative AI tools can augment learning and may be a technology thatstudents will use in the future, but their use may not be relevant or appropriate in all situations.Evaluate how using AI or learning about AI fits with a course’s goals and objectives.
units.why: Instructors should 'evaluate how using AI or learning about AI fits with a course's goals and objectives', so AI decisions follow learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: This course policy is driven by the learning goals and desiredlearning outcomes for the course: [insert description of learning goals and outcomes]The following actions are prohibited: ● entering all or any part of an assignment statement or test questions as part of a prompt to alarge language model AI tool; ● incorporating any part of an AI-written response in an assignment; ● using AI to summarize or contextualize reading assignments or source materials; and ● submitting your own work for this class to a large language model AI tool for iteration orimprovement.
units.why: The no-AI sample says 'This course policy is driven by the learning goals and desired learning outcomes for the course', tying the rule to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Be intentional about when AI use is appropriate. Do not use AI if it does not align with the assignment’s purpose.
units.why: "Do not use AI if it does not align with the assignment's purpose" tells students to judge fit to the assignment's learning aim, so P83 and a restriction.
units.fit_note: Frames fit with the assignment's purpose, not formal learning objectives.

units.passage: Policies are more effective when they are grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals of the course.
units.policy: Policies are more effective when they are grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals of the course.
units.why: Says policies should be 'grounded in pedagogical reasoning and tied to the specific learning goals': AI decisions follow learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: How do you want students to engage with GenAI in your course: What are skills and knowledge that you need students to practice, apply, and develop on their own? What aspects of their learning could be supplemented by GenAI?
units.why: The first guiding question asks which 'skills and knowledge' students must 'practice, apply, and develop on their own'. It ties AI decisions to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated, and each activity, assignment and exam are connected back to those learning objectives.
units.why: "Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated, and each activity, assignment and exam are connected back" ties assessment to learning objectives, which matches P83.
units.fit_note: Presented as an anti-cheating mastery design, not specifically about deciding AI use. Also (second coder): Presented as a mastery-orientation tip, not tied to AI permission.

units.passage: Update your learning objectives. Cognitive offloading is already a thing (e.g., you write down your grocery list so you won’t forget what to buy; our students, and we, use grammar and spell checks in email and paper generating software) and what can be cognitively offloaded will expand quickly with artificial intelligence. So, rethink your learning objectives by considering – which ones are easy (or even make sense) to cognitively offload to artificial intelligence.
units.why: "rethink your learning objectives by considering ... which ones are easy ... to cognitively offload to artificial intelligence" asks instructors to align learning objectives with what AI can do, matching P83.

units.passage: Think about your course objectives. What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance? When should students rely on AI assistance? Where can an AI aid facilitate a better outcome? Are new rubrics and assignment descriptions needed?
units.policy: Instructors think about their course objectives, including what cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance.
units.why: "Think about your course objectives. What are the cognitive tasks students need to perform without AI assistance?" ties AI decisions to learning objectives, P83.

units.passage: Let your learning outcomes be your guide: Any choices you make about preventing, allowing, or even requiring AI use should be in support of students meeting learning outcomes.
units.why: "Let your learning outcomes be your guide" says any choice to prevent, allow or require AI should support learning outcomes, which is P83.

units.passage: Consistent with academic rights and responsibilities, individual faculty shall ensure that AI use aligns with academic standards, disciplinary norms, institutional practices, and pedagogical goals.
units.why: "individual faculty shall ensure that AI use aligns with academic standards, disciplinary norms, institutional practices, and pedagogical goals" makes faculty responsible for fitting AI to pedagogical goals (P83).
units.fit_note: Also names academic standards, disciplinary norms and institutional practices, not only learning objectives.

units.passage: In these cases, we advise that you clearly describe how gen AI use meets the learning goals of the assignment and take into consideration accessibility parameters
units.why: "clearly describe how gen AI use meets the learning goals of the assignment" ties required AI use to learning goals, P83.

units.passage: The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning objectives . Below are several examples you can adopt or adapt
units.policy: The right AI syllabus statement for a course depends on that course's specific learning objectives.
units.why: "The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning objectives" ties the AI rule to course goals, so P83.

units.passage: One useful question to ask might be this: “How am I ensuring that the use of AI in my course promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking and learning that should derive from a university education?
units.why: Type: A P83, B P41. The reflective question asks whether AI use 'promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking and learning that should derive from a university education', which ties AI decisions to learning aims (P83). It does not say that AI shortcuts practice (P41). Fit note kept.
units.fit_note: A reflective question about higher-order thinking rather than a stated link to objectives. Framed as a reflective question to instructors rather than a limit on students.

units.passage: how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn.
units.why: "how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn" ties the AI rules to learning goals, which is P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).

units.passage: Connect the choice to your course learning objectives
units.why: "Connect the choice to your course learning objectives" tells instructors to base the choice of AI tool on learning goals, which is P83.

units.passage: Executive summary Section 1: Introduction Section 2: Generative AI capabilities and limitations Section 3: Guidelines and recommendations for educational settings Section 3.1: Academic integrity and accessibility Section 3.1.1: Prohibiting GAI tools Section 3.1.2: Attribution authorship, access and accountability in the use of GAI Section 3.2: Encouraging the responsible use of GAI tools Sections 3.3: Use of GAI by instructors for course content creation Section 4: Recommendations for faculty and administration Section 5: Conclusions Appendix A: State of the art in Generative AI Appendix B: Courses that develop writing as a skill Appendix C: Creative courses for music, literature, and art Appendix D: Courses in social sciences Appendix E: Mathematics, physical sciences, and engineering Appendix F: Courses in programming Appendix G: Courses in law Executive summary Educators must take generative artificial intelligence (GAI) into account when considering the learning objectives for their classes, since these technologies will not only be present in the future workplace, but are already being used by students.
units.why: This sentence states why AI must be considered in course design: 'since these technologies will not only be present in the future workplace, but are already being used by students.' It ties AI decisions to learning objectives, so P83 fits better than P44, which is about teaching AI as a career skill.

units.passage: We strongly encourage instructors to integrate GAI into learning outcomes to focus student education on higher-level learning objectives, critical thinking, and the skills and knowledge that they will need in the future.
units.why: The committee 'strongly encourage[s] instructors to integrate GAI into learning outcomes'. It asks instructors to build AI into outcomes, which is closer to P83 (decisions follow learning objectives) than to P79 (requiring AI use in coursework).

units.passage: To address these risks and take advantage of these opportunities, instructors should reassess learning outcomes for each class in light of the advent of GAI.
units.why: 'Instructors should reassess learning outcomes for each class' in light of GAI, aligning AI decisions with objectives; P83 rather than P35 because it concerns outcomes, not assignment redesign.

units.passage: Faculty are encouraged to identify well-defined learning outcomes to provide rationales for how and when GAI can/cannot be used in a particular course.
units.why: Faculty 'are encouraged to identify well-defined learning outcomes to provide rationales for how and when GAI can/cannot be used'. Rules follow learning objectives, so P83.

units.passage: For these reasons, we recommend that Cornell adopt a forward-looking approach that incorporates the use or non-use of GAI specifically into learning objectives.
units.why: The conclusion recommends Cornell 'adopt a forward-looking approach that incorporates the use or non-use of GAI specifically into learning objectives'. Rules follow learning objectives, so P83.

units.passage: Every College of Engineering course syllabus should have a GenAI policy statement that is consistent with the learning objectives of the course.
units.policy: The GenAI policy statement in each syllabus is consistent with the learning objectives of the course.
units.why: The required statement must be 'consistent with the learning objectives of the course', so AI rules follow learning objectives: P83.

units.passage: Learning Outcomes and Assessment Strategies Modify the course learning outcomes and assessment strategies to specify what students should be able to know and accomplish without the assistance from GenAI.
units.why: The page says to 'Modify the course learning outcomes and assessment strategies to specify what students should be able to know and accomplish without the assistance from GenAI'. Outcomes drive the rules, so P83.

units.passage: Am I adopting a policy that aligns with my own teaching preferences and goals for the course? Ultimately, these goals should be formalized as student learning outcomes.
units.why: "Am I adopting a policy that aligns with my own teaching preferences and goals ... formalized as student learning outcomes" ties the AI rule to learning outcomes, so P83; should in effect.

units.passage: writing student learning objectives (SLOs) prior to designing assessments helps ensure instructors are aligning
units.why: 'writing student learning objectives (SLOs) prior to designing assessments' ties assessment to objectives, applied to AI by 'Ensure Alignment with Learning Objectives' (P83).
units.fit_note: Generic backward-design advice, not explicit about whether AI is allowed.

units.passage: When AI is introduced in an assignment or course, instructors may need to differentiate between AI capabilities and human skills, as noted in Bloom’s Taxonomy Revisited .
units.why: 'instructors may need to differentiate between AI capabilities and human skills' links AI decisions to course learning goals (P83).

units.passage: Understanding and applying academic and professional standards for AI use, checking work, evaluating sources, and communicating clearly – these are high-level learning outcomes. Embrace them.
units.why: 'Understanding and applying academic and professional standards for AI use ... these are high-level learning outcomes. Embrace them.' frames AI use as learning goals (P83).
units.fit_note: Frames professional AI standards as outcomes, not a rule. | Professional standards as learning outcomes.

units.passage: Rather than starting with the final decision (e.g., should students use AI or not?), start with your learning goals and work backward from there.
units.why: The page says policy design is 'best approached as a pedagogical design decision' where one should 'start with your learning goals and work backward', tying AI rules to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Ideally, your course and assignment policies will help to focus student efforts on the core learning activities involved.
units.why: Policies should 'help to focus student efforts on the core learning activities', again linking AI rules to what students must learn (P83).

units.passage: Which tasks represent critical learning moments , where productive struggle , decision-making, or sense-making will benefit students and/or represent demonstration of core learning outcomes?
units.why: Instructors are asked which tasks are 'critical learning moments' where 'productive struggle' matters, i.e. where doing the work without AI builds skill; nearest is P41.
units.fit_note: It is a question to the instructor, not a statement that AI undermines learning.

units.passage: Which tasks are necessary but not central to your learning goals (e.g., proofreading, formatting)? Could use of generative AI tools for these tasks free your students up to focus on deeper thinking?
units.why: "Which tasks are necessary but not central to your learning goals (e.g., proofreading, formatting)? Could use of generative AI tools ... free your students up" suggests allowing AI on peripheral tasks, so P91 (editing and proofreading help), phrased as a question to instructors.
units.fit_note: Also frames the choice as freeing students to focus on deeper thinking.

units.passage: Which tasks are necessary but not central to your learning goals (e.g., proofreading, formatting)? Could use of generative AI tools for these tasks free your students up to focus on deeper thinking? Which tasks are new to students , and with which do they already have experience?
units.why: "Which tasks are new to students, and with which do they already have experience?" tells instructors to consider student experience when setting the rule, so P83 with a note (it echoes P42, but gives no rule for novices).
units.fit_note: The consideration is student experience, a part of learning-goal alignment. / Student experience, not only learning objectives, is a factor.

units.passage: Ultimately, instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool would help their students meet those targets.
units.policy: Instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool would help their students meet those targets.
units.why: "instructors should consider their course learning objectives and whether a specific AI writing tool would help their students meet those targets" ties the AI decision to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: When establishing your policies on AI use, keep your course goals and values in mind. Consider how your students will get the most out of their learning experience and if there are opportunities for your students to use and learn about AI that align with the learning objectives of the course.
units.why: "keep your course goals and values in mind" and "align with the learning objectives of the course" ties AI decisions to learning objectives: P83.

units.passage: Connect your course policies to your course's learning outcomes and explain how these guidelines support both academic integrity and skill development.
units.why: "Connect your course policies to your course's learning outcomes" bases AI decisions on learning outcomes, P83.

units.passage: Align AI use with your course learning objectives.
units.why: "Align AI use with your course learning objectives" bases AI decisions on objectives; P83.

units.passage: This Center for Teaching handbook explores the questions that generative AI raises for teaching and learning, encouraging instructors to make intentional decisions that align with their learning goals, disciplinary context, and teaching values while remaining focused on supporting student learning.
units.why: The Center for Teaching handbook encourages "intentional decisions that align with their learning goals, disciplinary context, and teaching values"; P83.

units.passage: Effective assessments are closely aligned to course goals and allow students to demonstrate their learning in authentic ways.
units.why: "Effective assessments are closely aligned to course goals and allow students to demonstrate their learning in authentic ways" bases assessment design on goals; P83.

units.passage: No matter your position on the use of so-called AI in the classroom, I recommend that you consider first your course goals and whether and how any given technology might undermine or support your students in the process of meeting those goals
units.policy: No matter your position on the use of so-called AI in the classroom, I recommend that you consider first your course goals and whether and how any given technology might undermine or support your students in the process of meeting those goals.
units.why: English advice: 'consider first your course goals and whether and how any given technology might undermine or support your students' asks instructors to base AI decisions on course goals, P83.

units.passage: Course policies regarding the use of generative AI are best adapted to the local context of the course, including the instructor’s expertise and perspectives; the course learning goals; the nature of the coursework, discipline and/or profession; and the learning needs of the students
units.why: The Adaptability paragraph says policies are 'best adapted to the local context of the course', including learning goals and discipline, so AI rules follow course learning goals (P83).
units.fit_note: Also lists instructor expertise, discipline and tool modality as inputs, not only learning objectives. | Also says policies reflect the instructor's expertise and perspectives, so each instructor decides (P04).

units.passage: Ethical engagement with GAI, including restrictions, guardrails, or complete integration of GAI into assignments, will vary significantly across disciplines, and even among classes and individual faculty, depending on the skills and learning outcomes they seek to impart.
units.why: Rules vary "depending on the skills and learning outcomes they seek to impart", tying AI decisions to learning outcomes (P83).

units.passage: in accordance with their targeted course, major, and/or minor outcomes.
units.why: Incorporation should follow 'their targeted course, major, and/or minor outcomes'; AI decisions tied to learning objectives, P83.

units.passage: Faculty retain the autonomy to align AI use with course learning objectives and disciplinary norms, using the traffic light model as a decision support tool
units.why: The Pedagogical Choice principle says faculty "align AI use with course learning objectives and disciplinary norms"; the alignment criterion makes this P83, not just P04.

units.passage: Contextualize GenAI by highlighting the disciplinary uses of these tools, course-specific aims and goals for GenAI use, and the relationship of GenAI use to student learning outcomes (course-based, curricular, or institutional).
units.why: Instructors can explain "the relationship of GenAI use to student learning outcomes", tying AI decisions to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Depending on your context, generative AI may serve as a learning tool or as an obstacle in helping students reach your course goals.
units.why: "generative AI may serve as a learning tool or as an obstacle" says AI can help or hinder course goals. It sets no rule but links the instructor choice to course goals; P83 fits best.
units.fit_note: Frames AI as a tool or obstacle relative to course goals; does not require the decision to follow stated learning objectives.

units.passage: You should always begin with your learning objectives when considering what policy to adopt and use in your course.
units.why: "You should always begin with your learning objectives when considering what policy to adopt" ties the policy to objectives, P83.

units.passage: The goal(s) of the educational experience.
units.policy: Each unit policy states the goals of the educational experience.
units.why: 'The goal(s) of the educational experience' must be stated, tying AI rules to objectives, so P83.
units.fit_note: Requires stating goals, not explicitly that AI rules follow from them.

units.passage: It is possible and perhaps expected that different capstone experiences (for example, a PhD dissertation and a non-thesis Master’s project) will have unique goals; thus, different AI guidelines.
units.policy: Different capstone experiences, for example a PhD dissertation and a non-thesis Master's project, will have unique goals and thus different AI guidelines.
units.why: "different capstone experiences ... will have unique goals; thus, different AI guidelines" ties guidelines to goals, P83.

units.passage: Lead with learning outcomes and disciplinary values, not with the motivation to curb cheating or protect academic integrity.
units.why: "Lead with learning outcomes and disciplinary values, not with the motivation to curb cheating" ties the AI decision to learning goals, so P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).
units.fit_note: Also says to lead with learning rather than cheating prevention and that integrity is a tool for inquiry.

units.passage: Consider if GenAI can scaffold or not scaffold learning in these areas and how they affirm disciplinary values students should learn.
units.why: "Consider if GenAI can scaffold or not scaffold learning in these areas" asks instructors to decide AI use by whether it supports learning, P83 again; kept as a separate unit because it states a second test (scaffolding).

units.passage: Students must not use AI to bypass key learning objectives of the class.
units.why: "Students must not use AI to bypass key learning objectives of the class" bans AI use that undercuts learning goals; nearest P83 (align with learning objectives), though here it is a prohibition on students.
units.fit_note: A student-facing prohibition, whereas P83 is about how decisions are made.

units.passage: You are welcome/expected to use generative AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Dall-e, etc.) in this class as doing so aligns with the course learning goal [insert the course learning goal use of AI aligns with].
units.why: Permission is justified because it "aligns with the course learning goal", tying AI use to learning objectives, P83.

units.passage: Stronger statements will also include language tailored to the academic values of your discipline and pedagogy.
units.why: Says stronger statements should be 'tailored to the academic values of your discipline and pedagogy', so rules follow the course's aims (P83).
units.fit_note: Ties the statement to the academic values of the discipline and pedagogy, not to course learning outcomes.

units.passage: For example, in a creative writing course, you might focus on originality and voice; in a coding class, collaboration with tools might be part of the process.
units.why: 'in a coding class, collaboration with tools might be part of the process' is an example, in the same sentence as the discipline-tailoring advice, of what a statement might say. It is an illustration, not a rule, so it is coded informs under P83 (align with the discipline), not as a default stance.

units.passage: The educational purpose of AI usage and how they relate to the courses learning outcomes
units.why: A syllabus statement should tie AI use to learning outcomes: P83.

units.passage: Taking some time to reflect on your learning goals for students can help lead you to a policy that fits with your instructional style and teaching philosophy.
units.why: 'Taking some time to reflect on your learning goals for students can help lead you to a policy' ties the AI rule to learning goals, P83.

units.passage: Think carefully about whether you can confidently assert that students have met the objectives for your course if they use AI.
units.why: 'whether you can confidently assert that students have met the objectives for your course if they use AI' makes learning objectives the test for permitting AI, P83.

units.passage: Does your policy ensure that students can think flexibly and apply coursework in response to real-world future challenges?
units.why: 'Does your policy ensure that students can think flexibly and apply coursework' ties the policy to critical thinking as a learning objective, P83.
units.fit_note: Names critical thinking as a goal the policy should protect, not a decision rule. | Stated as a design check about critical thinking, not as a limit on AI use.

units.passage: Faculty views toward acceptable use of AI are influenced by course and assignment learning goals, amongst other factors,
units.why: "Faculty views toward acceptable use of AI are influenced by course and assignment learning goals" says the decision should follow learning goals, P83, informs.

units.passage: Using these tools aligns with the course learning outcomes/student goals [ insert the course learning goal(s) that use of AI aligns with
units.why: "Using these tools aligns with the course learning outcomes" ties permission to learning goals, P83, informs.

units.passage: Faculty should consider how using or restricting AI will help students meet learning outcomes.
units.why: Faculty "should consider how using or restricting AI will help students meet learning outcomes", so AI rules follow outcomes, P83.

units.passage: Since writing, analytical, and critical thinking skills are part of the learning outcomes of this course, all writing assignments should be prepared by the student.
units.why: The Creative Writing sample ties its rule to 'learning outcomes', so AI rules follow the course objectives (P83).

units.passage: 1. Align AI Use with Course Learning Goals AI can help students achieve some learning goals while hindering others. As the use of AI becomes more common within a discipline or professional field, students may need to practice using AI tools to complete work related to some learning goals, whereas they may need to avoid its use to acquire foundational knowledge and skills
units.why: "AI can help students achieve some learning goals while hindering others" is the rationale for aligning AI use with course learning goals (P83); it states a fact, so informs, addressed to instructors designing the course.

units.passage: The most important thing to consider is to align AI use with the course’s learning goals
units.why: "The most important thing to consider is to align AI use with the course's learning goals" repeats that learning goals drive AI decisions, P83; it is coded again because it is an FAQ answer that adds the university AI Policy governs.

units.passage: State your general stance and the rationale tied to learning outcomes in your syllabus; note privacy considerations.
units.why: The rationale is to be 'tied to learning outcomes', aligning AI decisions with objectives (P83).

units.passage: where you may also be asked to share your prompts, screenshots of your chats with Generative AI tools, and how you used Generative AI to prepare you to, by the end of the semester, independently (without the use of Generative AI) achieve the learning objectives of this course.
units.why: Open use is meant to prepare students to 'independently (without the use of Generative AI) achieve the learning objectives'; AI use tied to learning objectives (P83).
units.fit_note: Frames AI use as preparing students to meet course objectives independently.

units.passage: Have a syllabus policy statement on what AI use is allowed, decided at your own or your unit's discretion based on the course's learning objectives.
units.policy: The decision on what AI use is allowed is based on the course's learning objectives
units.why: The sentence ties the decision to "the course's learning objectives", so the rule on how to decide follows objectives (P83), not just who decides.

units.passage: A good AI policy is learning-centered and transparent, whatever stance it takes. It names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it, in your specific course, and it says so clearly enough that students don't have to guess their way through grey areas.
units.policy: A good AI policy names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it, in the specific course
units.why: The policy "names what students can learn from working with AI, or from working without it": a good policy follows from the specific learning objective, which is P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).

units.passage: The AI uses you allow or prohibit should reflect the kinds of thinking students need to do to achieve learning goals.
units.why: "Center your policies on learning. The AI uses you allow or prohibit should reflect the kinds of thinking students need to do" ties AI decisions to learning goals (P83).

units.passage: Consider that the impact of AI use will vary by task, enhancing some activities while hindering learning in others. Design your policies with this in mind.
units.why: "the impact of AI use will vary by task, enhancing some activities while hindering learning in others" asks instructors to fit rules to tasks; closest is P83 but it concerns tasks rather than stated learning objectives.
units.fit_note: Ties rules to the task asked of students, not to formal learning objectives. | Task-level reasoning about whether AI helps or hinders learning.

units.passage: The goal of this task is to produce evidence of your unaided critical thinking, not to evaluate the quality of your writing. I am interested in your ability to develop and communicate your original ideas, even if they are not fully polished in the limited time allotted for this exercise.
units.why: "The goal of this task is to produce evidence of your unaided critical thinking, not to evaluate the quality of your writing" explains the assessment aim for the no-AI rule; P83 ties the rule to the task goal.
units.fit_note: Reason is that the task must show unaided thinking; this is the explanation given to students inside an example assignment policy.

units.passage: expectations for individual assignments may vary based on the learning goals of each task.
units.why: "Your expectations for individual assignments may vary based on the learning goals of each task" ties AI rules to learning goals (P83).

units.passage: nivel de autorización o permiso para el uso de las herramientas de IA que mejor correspondan con los objetivos del curso.
units.why: The level chosen should "correspondan con los objetivos del curso", tying AI decisions to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: Instructors should use course learning outcomes to determine when students must, may, or cannot use GenAI.
units.why: Instructors "should use course learning outcomes to determine when students must, may, or cannot use GenAI", tying AI decisions to objectives: P83. The must/may/cannot wording resembles P05 but no named tiers are defined.

units.passage: Likewise, instructors should use course learning outcomes to evaluate their own use of GenAI in their teaching.

units.why: Says how AI is handled 'varies based on course, discipline, and industry contexts and related learning outcomes'; the choice follows learning outcomes, P83.

units.passage: The faculty have a responsibility to weigh the humanistic, ethical, and pedagogical considerations when determining how and whether to integrate AI into their instruction to ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning, is accessible to students, and will do more good than harm in the short and long term.
units.why: Faculty weigh considerations 'to ensure that AI is facilitating and not replacing learning'; a learning-based criterion for faculty decisions, nearest P83.
units.fit_note: States a criterion (AI facilitates, does not replace, learning) rather than naming specific learning objectives.

units.passage: While Generative AI can enhance learning in some contexts, its use is viewed as counter to the specific learning objectives of this course. (Define which learning objectives AI would impact)

units.passage: To begin with, think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the learning goals of your course.
units.why: Asks instructors to 'think about whether the use of generative AI tools in your course would support the learning goals'; AI decisions follow learning goals, P83.

units.passage: It is important to examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable AI policy, since learning outcomes are what students should know and be able to do by the end of the course.
units.why: 'It is important to examine the learning outcomes of your courses and adopt a suitable AI policy'; policy follows outcomes, P83.

units.passage: The educational value of using AI-generated or AI-curated content depends on factors like the subject, students' learning needs, instructors' pedagogical approaches and preferences, and course and assessment design.
units.why: The text says educational value 'depends on factors like the subject, students' learning needs, instructors' pedagogical approaches and preferences, and course and assessment design', so allowed use depends on course context; P83 is the nearest type (follow from course aims), though it names more factors than objectives.
units.fit_note: Lists several context factors (subject, learner needs, pedagogy, assessment), not only learning objectives. / The text names subject, learner needs and instructor preferences, not learning objectives specifically.

units.passage: Alignment with learning goals
units.policy: Instructors crafting a course AI policy take into account alignment with learning goals.
units.why: The bullet 'Alignment with learning goals' lists a consideration for course policy; it ties AI decisions to learning objectives, so P83.

units.passage: For example, if your course focuses on building students’ critical reading skills, you might state that students are not allowed to use generative AI to summarize course readings.
units.policy: If a course focuses on building critical reading skills, the instructor might state that students may not use generative AI to summarize course readings.
units.why: 'if your course focuses on building students' critical reading skills, you might state that students are not allowed to use generative AI to summarize course readings' ties the rule to learning objectives, P83.

units.passage: At the same time, the incorporation of GenAI in academic settings must ensure policies and guidelines exist to preserve the mission of the University by fostering academic integrity and promoting critical thinking, while aligning with the associated learning objectives of student coursework and programs
units.why: The Purpose section says the incorporation of GenAI must align "with the associated learning objectives of student coursework and programs". It is a general principle (informs) addressed to the whole community, tying AI decisions to learning objectives, so P83.

units.passage: Any allowed use of GenAI use must ensure course learning objectives are met as allowable within this guideline or any further college or department level restrictions.
units.why: "Any allowed use of GenAI use must ensure course learning objectives are met" ties permitted use to learning objectives (P83).

units.passage: To that end, you are welcome to use generative AI tools in this class as long as it aligns with the learning outcomes or goals associated with assignments.
units.why: Sample: 'you are welcome to use generative AI tools in this class as long as it aligns with the learning outcomes or goals associated with assignments'; permission tied to learning objectives, P83.
units.fit_note: Also a default permission (P02).

units.passage: GenAI should support learning goals.
units.why: "GenAI should support learning goals" ties AI use to learning goals, P83.

units.passage: The policy may be customized to align with your syllabus specific learning goals.
units.why: "may be customized to align with your syllabus specific learning goals" says the course policy should follow the course's learning goals, P83.

units.passage: Misuse of AI tools, including use of AI that undermines the student learning objectives of the course or assignment, failing to cite AI-generated content, relying too heavily on AI for work completion [as defined above in permitted use], or submitting inaccurate information generated by AI tools,
units.why: "use of AI that undermines the student learning objectives of the course or assignment" counts as misuse, tying AI limits to learning objectives, P83.
units.fit_note: Uses learning objectives as the test for misuse. Uses objectives as a test for misuse rather than for deciding what is allowed.

units.passage: Review the university’s recommendations to guide faculty through developing a course policy that aligns with the course learning goals and generative AI. These can be augmented to work across various contexts.

units.passage: As you update your syllabus, consider how your assessments and learning activities support your learning outcomes while preparing students for real-world application.
units.why: "consider how your assessments and learning activities support your learning outcomes" ties assessment choices to learning outcomes, P83.

units.passage: Is this genAI tool appropriate for your learning goals?

units.passage: “[t]he permitted use of AI may vary from course to course and assignment to assignment based on the specific learning outcomes of the course or assignment.”
units.policy: AI permission is based on the specific learning outcomes of the course or assignment.

units.passage: “[t]he permitted use of AI may vary from course to course and assignment to assignment based on the specific learning outcomes of the course or assignment.”
units.policy: AI permission is based on the specific learning outcomes of the course or assignment.

units.passage: Alignment with learning goals

units.passage: Approval will be granted based on the appropriateness and educational value of the proposed use.

units.passage: Ensure that AI-assisted teaching does not compromise learning objectives

units.passage: How does my stance on AI align with my course learning outcomes?

units.passage: As faculty evaluate whether generative AI has a place in their curricula, we encourage them to explore various generative AI tools' potential benefits and shortcomings to see how they align with and advance the faculty's learning objectives.

units.passage: Review your course learning objectives and consider whether AI tools might support these at various stages

units.passage: We recognize that this is an evolving space, and we encourage you to approach this as an opportunity to align your course policies with your learning goals and values as educators.

units.passage: Faculty are encouraged to determine whether AI use is appropriate for their course, assignments, or assessments based on their learning objectives, subject‑area considerations, and professional context

units.passage: Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives—not override them. By designing assignments that emphasize real-world application, critical thinking, and student reflection, instructors can help students engage with AI tools responsibly while still demonstrating their own understanding and originality.
units.why: 'Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives—not override them' ties AI decisions to learning goals: P83.

units.passage: The syllabus statements in this collection are examples that instructors can use as they set and communicate boundaries for student AI use that align with their course goals and teaching values.

units.passage: Always ensure that your Gen AI resources/materials support your course objectives/outcomes.
